messages.author: fde4048c840328bf
messages.subject: Constraining parameters in stationary models
parts:
Hi all!

I was wondering if it is possible to constrain the parameters when there are several restrictions that should be met. For example, in a stationary autoregressive process of order 2, 

Y(t) =phi1*Y(t-1) + phi2*(t-2)

we want that,

phi1 + phi2 < 1
phi1 - phi2 < 1
abs(phi2) < 1

The third constraint is not a problem, as we can just do,
real<lower=-1,upper=1>phi2;

And, if we had only one constraint (for example, the first one), we could use a transformation,
parameters{

real<upper=1> phi12;
real<lower=-1, upper=1> phi2;

}

transformed parameters{

real phi1;
phi1 <- 1-phi2;

}

but, how can I impose the other restriction?

More generally, if we have an autoregressive process of order P, is it possible to restrict the roots of the p-th order polynomial to lie outside the unit circle?

Thanks!

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Constraining parameters in stationary models
parts: On 3/7/13 1:49 PM, Carlos wrote:> Hi all!

>
> I was wondering if it is possible to constrain the parameters when there
> are several restrictions that should be met.
> For example, in a stationary autoregressive process of order 2,
>
> Y(t) =phi1*Y(t-1) + phi2*(t-2)
>
> we want that,
>
> phi1 + phi2 < 1
> phi1 - phi2< 1
> abs(phi2) < 1

Funny you should bring that up. I've had it on our
to-do list for a while. When I asked Andrew, he suggested
it would be a bad idea to do this because the data should
constrain the solution to be stationary if the process
actually is stationary and you don't want to constrain it to
a stationary solution if it's not.

I'm more interested in what you can do with Stan, not whether
it's a good idea statistically :-)

The stationary constraints above are captured by:

real <lower=-1,upper=1> phi2;
real <upper=(1 - fabs(phi2))> phi1;

The constraint on phi2 is the one you pointed out. The
second pair of equations can be rewritten as:

phi1 < 1 - phi2
phi1 < 1 + phi2

and we know

1 - abs(phi2) = min(1 - phi2, 1 + phi2).

> More generally, if we have an autoregressive process of order P,
> is it possible to restrict the roots of the p-th order
> polynomial to lie outside the unit circle?

But if you really want to do this, one approach is to
parameterize in terms of the roots and then define the
coefficients as transformed parameters.

But if you want priors on the coefficients
instead of the roots, you need to add the log absolute determinant
of the Jacobian to lp__.

Both of these calcs gets messy at higher orders.

Or maybe priors on the roots will suggest different models?
What Andrew calls the Pinocchio Principle.

- Bob

parts:
Funny you should bring that up.  I've had it on our 
to-do list for a while.  When I asked Andrew, he suggested 
it would be a bad idea to do this because the data should 
constrain the solution to be stationary if the process 
actually is stationary and you don't want to constrain it to 
a stationary solution if it's not.

Well, I think that Andrew has a very good point  here :D But... at least my experience is that when you have highly autocorrelated processes (let's say, an AR(1) model with phi=0.9), if I put a non-constrained prior, and I allow the support to be R, even if in general the chain of the parameter is inside (-1,1), sometimes there are outliers such that abs(phi)>1. If we want to focus on means, ok, that is not a problem. But if we want to compute impulse response functions, and want to extract the quantiles by simulation, sometimes the paths explode, and I think that might be difficult to extract good conclusions about them. Also, I was thinking in more complicated models, like a Vector Autorregression. Even if the data is stationary, it is quite difficult to extract draws from a conjugate prior (multivariate normal distribution and an Inverse Wishart) such that the draw leads to a stationary path. I think that Gary Koop has a paper on that (he finds the rejection rate to be around 90% or more in a standard Gibbs Sampler, such that he discards any draw that does not lead to a stationary process).   But this is just given my (little) experience :D

The stationary constraints above are captured by: 

   real <lower=-1,upper=1> phi2; 
   real <upper=(1 - fabs(phi2))> phi1; 

The constraint on phi2 is the one you pointed out.  The 
second pair of equations can be rewritten as: 

    phi1 < 1 - phi2 
    phi1 < 1 + phi2 

and we know 

   1 - abs(phi2) = min(1 - phi2, 1 + phi2).
I didn't know that we can use parameters in the bounds!! This is very good news!.

But if you really want to do this, one approach is to parameterize in terms of the roots and then define the coefficients as transformed parameters. But if you want priors on the coefficients instead of the roots, you need to add the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian to lp__. Both of these calcs gets messy at higher orders.

Mmmm, I will probably have to think of this. If there are one-to-one mappings from the roots to the coefficients, should not be any problem, but I am not sure about that. In any case, as you said, I guess that the calcs will get terribly difficult...

Or maybe priors on the roots will suggest different models? 
What Andrew calls the Pinocchio Principle.

One way to implement this in Stan would be to define a new datatype for a vector which is in the AR stationarity and invertibility region. The function ARtransPars in the R package dlm maps between the reals and AR parameters using the method defined the following paper,

Jones, 1987. Randomly choosing parameters from the stationarity and invertibility region of autoregressive-moving average models. Applied Statistics, 36.
